q: The SI unit of angular displacement is the:
x: The radian is the SI unit of angular displacement. Degrees and revolutions also measure angles but are not SI units, and the metre measures length.

q: A particle moves 6 m along the arc of a circle of radius 2 m. Its angular displacement is:
x: θ = s/r = 6/2 = 3 rad. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 12 rad, and dividing the wrong way gives 0.33 rad.

q: The direction of a small angular displacement of a rotating body is:
o: Along the axis of rotation, given by the right-hand rule
Along the tangent to the circular path
Towards the centre of the circle
x: A small angular displacement is a vector along the axis of rotation; curling the fingers of the right hand in the sense of rotation, the thumb gives its direction. The tangent is the direction of linear velocity.

q: A wheel completes 5 revolutions. Its angular displacement is:
x: One revolution is 2π rad, so 5 revolutions are 5 × 2π = 10π rad. 1800 is the angle in degrees, not radians.

q: Points X (near the centre) and Y (near the rim) lie on a rotating rigid disc. In the same time interval:
o: Both travel the same arc length
X has a larger angular displacement than Y
Both have the same angular displacement, but Y travels a longer arc
Y has a larger angular displacement than X
x: Every point of a rigid body turns through the same angle. Arc length s = rθ is larger for Y because it is farther from the axis.

q: The radian has no dimensions because it is defined as the:
o: Product of arc length and radius
Ratio of an arc length to the radius
Ratio of the radius to the time taken
Number of degrees in one revolution
x: θ = s/r is a length divided by a length, so the radian is dimensionless. The other quantities either have dimensions or do not define the radian.

q: Through what angle does the minute hand of a clock turn in 20 minutes?
x: The minute hand makes one revolution (2π rad) in 60 min, so in 20 min it turns ⅓ × 2π = 2π/3 rad.

q: A body moves halfway round a circle of radius 7 m. Its angular displacement and the distance along the arc are (π = 22/7):
x: Half a revolution is π rad, and the arc length is s = rθ = 7 × 22/7 = 22 m. 14 m is the diameter, which is the straight-line displacement, not the arc length.

q: Angular displacement can be treated as a vector quantity only when it is:
x: Very small angular displacements add like vectors; large ones do not obey the vector law of addition, so they are not treated as vectors. The unit or sense of rotation does not decide this.

q: Angular displacement of a body moving in a circle is the:
o: Angle swept out by the radius line in a given time
Straight-line distance between the start and end points
Number of revolutions made per second
x: Angular displacement is the angle through which the radius joining the body to the centre turns. Arc length per second is linear speed, and revolutions per second is frequency.

q: One complete revolution is equal to:
x: In one revolution the arc length is the circumference 2πr, so θ = 2πr/r = 2π rad. π rad is half a revolution.

q: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the:
x: This is the definition of the radian: arc length equal to the radius gives θ = r/r = 1 rad. An arc equal to the diameter would give 2 rad.

q: One radian is approximately equal to:
x: 1 rad = 180°/π ≈ 57.3°. 180° is π rad, and 3.14 is the value of π, not of one radian in degrees.

q: An angle of 150° expressed in radians is:
An angle of 3π/2 rad is equal to:
x: Degrees = (3π/2) × (180°/π) = 270°, which is three-quarters of a revolution.

q: One degree is equal to:
x: 360° = 2π rad, so 1° = 2π/360 = π/180 rad ≈ 0.0175 rad. 180/π is the number of degrees in one radian.

q: Which shows the angles in correct increasing order of size?
x: 1 rad ≈ 57.3°, which is larger than 1° but smaller than 90°, and 1 revolution is 360°. So the order is 1°, 1 rad, 90°, 1 revolution.

q: The radius of a circle is doubled. In radians, one complete revolution round the new circle is:
x: θ = s/r: doubling r doubles the circumference too, so the ratio stays 2πr/r = 2π rad. The radian measure of an angle does not depend on the size of the circle.

q: An arc whose length equals the diameter of a circle subtends at the centre an angle of:
x: θ = s/r = 2r/r = 2 rad. An arc equal to the radius subtends 1 rad, and π rad needs an arc of half the circumference.

q: Which of the following angles is the largest?
x: 2 rad ≈ 2 × 57.3° ≈ 115°, while 0.25 revolution = 90° and 1.5 rad ≈ 86°. So 2 rad is larger than 100° and the others.

q: The SI unit of angular velocity is:
x: Angular velocity is angular displacement per unit time, so its SI unit is radian per second. rad s⁻² is the unit of angular acceleration, and m s⁻¹ is for linear velocity.

q: A body moving in a circle turns through 180° in 0.5 s. Its average angular velocity is:
x: 180° = π rad, so ω = θ/t = π/0.5 = 2π rad s⁻¹. 360 comes from dividing degrees by time and wrongly calling the result rad s⁻¹.

q: A body moves in a circle at constant speed and completes one revolution every 2 s. Its angular velocity is:
x: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2 = π rad s⁻¹. Multiplying 2π by T instead of dividing gives 4π rad s⁻¹.

q: A disc rotates anticlockwise in a horizontal plane, as seen from above. The direction of its angular velocity is:
o: Along the tangent to the rim
Towards the centre of the disc
x: By the right-hand rule, fingers curled anticlockwise (seen from above) make the thumb point upward along the axis. Angular velocity always lies along the axis of rotation.

q: Taking one rotation of the Earth about its axis as 24 hours, the Earth's angular velocity is:
x: ω = 2π/T with T = 24 × 3600 = 86400 s. 2π/24 is in rad per hour, not per second, and 2π/3600 would mean one turn per hour.

q: Which quantity has the same value for every point of a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis?
x: All points of a rigid body turn through the same angle in the same time, so they share one angular velocity. Linear speed v = rω and distance travelled both increase with distance from the axis.

q: The ratio of the angular velocity of the minute hand of a clock to that of its hour hand is:
x: The minute hand turns once in 1 h and the hour hand once in 12 h, so the minute hand is 12 times faster. 60 : 1 confuses this with the second hand and minute hand.

q: The dimensions of angular velocity are:
x: The radian is dimensionless, so rad s⁻¹ has dimensions of 1/time, [T⁻¹]. [LT⁻¹] is the dimension of linear velocity.

q: A wheel makes 120 revolutions per minute. Its angular velocity and its time period are:
x: 120 rev/min = 2 rev s⁻¹, so ω = 2π × 2 = 4π rad s⁻¹ and T = 1/f = 0.5 s. 240π results from forgetting to change minutes to seconds.

q: If the frequency of rotation of a wheel is doubled, its angular velocity:
x: ω = 2πf, so ω is directly proportional to the frequency. Doubling f doubles ω.

q: For a particle moving in a circle of radius r with angular speed ω, its linear speed v is given by:
x: Dividing s = rθ by the time taken gives v = rω. rω² is the formula for centripetal acceleration, not speed.

q: A wheel of radius 0.4 m rotates at 10 rad s⁻¹. The linear speed of a point on its rim is:
x: v = rω = 0.4 × 10 = 4 m s⁻¹. Dividing ω by r gives 25, and rω² = 40 is the centripetal acceleration in m s⁻².

q: A wheel of radius 0.5 m has an angular acceleration of 6 rad s⁻². The tangential acceleration of a point on its rim is:
x: aₜ = rα = 0.5 × 6 = 3 m s⁻². Dividing α by r gives 12 m s⁻², which is a common slip.

q: Two points on a rotating disc are 10 cm and 20 cm from the axis. The ratio of their linear speeds v₁ : v₂ is:
x: Both points have the same ω, and v = rω, so v is proportional to r: 10 : 20 = 1 : 2. Their angular speeds, not linear speeds, are in the ratio 1 : 1.

q: A wheel of radius 0.35 m rolls without slipping through 10 revolutions. The distance moved by the wheel is (π = 22/7):
x: θ = 10 × 2π rad, so s = rθ = 0.35 × 20 × 22/7 = 22 m. Using πr instead of 2πr per revolution gives 11 m.

q: The linear velocity of a particle moving in a circle is directed:
o: Towards the centre of the circle
Along the tangent to the circle
Away from the centre along the radius
x: Linear velocity v = ω × r is perpendicular to both the axis and the radius, so it lies along the tangent. The axis is the direction of angular velocity.

q: A wheel of radius 0.5 m starts from rest with a uniform angular acceleration of 2 rad s⁻². After 5 s, the linear speed of a point on its rim is:
x: ω = αt = 2 × 5 = 10 rad s⁻¹, then v = rω = 0.5 × 10 = 5 m s⁻¹. 10 is the angular speed, not the linear speed, and 1 m s⁻² is the tangential acceleration rα.

q: A car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ on wheels of radius 0.4 m that roll without slipping. The angular speed of each wheel is:
x: ω = v/r = 20/0.4 = 50 rad s⁻¹. Multiplying v by r gives 8, and dividing r by v gives 0.02.

q: Two pulleys of radii 10 cm and 30 cm are connected by a belt that does not slip, so their rims have the same linear speed. The small pulley turns at 9 rad s⁻¹. The large pulley turns at:
x: v = r₁ω₁ = r₂ω₂, so ω₂ = (10 × 9)/30 = 3 rad s⁻¹. Multiplying instead of dividing by the radius ratio gives 27 rad s⁻¹.
